issues.item: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: The profile is not coherent with a toxic chemical exposure trauma. The selected Threat items are dominated by interpersonal/being-followed danger themes ('someone is following me', lock checking) rather than contamination, health deterioration, environmental exposure, or bodily harm themes that would fit chemical exposure.

issues.item: Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked
issues.explanation: The Maladaptive Strategy item 'Never Alone' is also strongly interpersonal/assault-focused and is hard to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure. 'Avoid Conflict' similarly targets confrontation rather than exposure-related danger, and is not plausibly linked to the selected Threat items or trauma type.

issues.item: Never Alone: make sure never to be alone with another person
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, 'Never Alone with another person' is hard to reconcile clinically: it implies fear of interpersonal danger rather than contamination, bodily harm, or environmental exposure. No Trigger, Memory, or Appraisal items support an interpersonal-assault formulation.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Conflict' also points to interpersonal threat management rather than consequences of chemical exposure. With no corroborating interpersonal threat, appraisal, or memory content, this strategy appears misaligned with the trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Conflict: Any situation that might involve disagreement or confrontation
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, avoiding conflict is not a plausible trauma-linked maladaptive strategy unless supported by appraisals about blame, authority, or interpersonal danger, which are absent here. It appears clinically disconnected from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone is hard to reconcile with the stated threat pattern. The threat items emphasize generalized unsafety and checking the physical environment, but not collapse, contamination, or medical emergency fears that would make solitude specifically dangerous after chemical exposure.

vignette:
Tien is a 52-year-old HVAC technician, married for twenty-eight years, who lives with his wife in a modest ranch house on the outskirts of a small Midwestern city. For most of his career, he worked commercial jobs-schools, office parks, warehouses-often in mechanical rooms where chemical solvents and refrigerants pooled in the air. Two years ago, during a routine maintenance call at a shuttered plastics plant, a corroded valve burst while he was replacing a condenser coil. A cloud of methylene chloride vapor engulfed him for perhaps thirty seconds before he could scramble out. He coughed, his eyes burned, and his supervisor dismissed it as a minor leak. But Tien spent that night in the ER with dizziness and chest tightness, and for weeks afterward he could not shake the feeling that something inside him had been poisoned.

That feeling never really left. At first, he tried to reason with himself-the doctors had cleared him, the air in the plant had been tested, the incident was over. But his body refused to cooperate. His shoulders stayed hunched, his jaw clenched, his hands cold with sweat even when he sat in his own living room. He began checking the front door lock three, four times before bed, then the windows, then the back door again. His wife would call out from the bedroom, "Tien, it's fine," and he would nod, but the words did not reach the part of him that kept scanning. He had come to believe that danger was not something that announced itself-it was silent, invisible, and it had nearly killed him once without warning. What frightened him most was the thought that he might not recognize safety even if it were right in front of him.

Over the months that followed, Tien's daily life contracted around this belief. He stopped relaxing-completely. If he found himself sitting still after dinner, his mind would immediately conjure the smell of solvent, the tightness in his chest, and he would get up, find a task, anything to stay in motion. Relaxing felt dangerous, as though letting his guard down would invite another exposure. He also began avoiding anything he considered stressful: he turned down overtime, stopped answering calls from unfamiliar numbers, and let his wife handle all the household decisions. Being alone in a room-or worse, in an empty building-became unbearable. When he arrived at a job site, he kept the service bay door propped open and left the radio loud, needing some sign of other people nearby. His body stayed constantly on alert, a low hum of tension that never fully shut off. He could not sit through a meal without his leg jittering under the table.

The most demanding part of his week was still the work itself. He had to enter mechanical rooms, crawl through crawlspaces, and handle chemicals every day. He now wore a respirator even for jobs that required only a dust mask, and he checked his equipment three times before starting. His supervisor noticed the slowdown; Tien had been passed over for a lead technician position he had once been a natural candidate for. His wife noticed too-the way he flinched when she opened the oven, the way he insisted on double-checking the stove knobs before they left the house. She asked if he wanted to talk to someone, and Tien said no, he was managing. But he was not managing. He was spending so much energy avoiding danger that he had almost no energy left for anything else.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a small thing: a whiff of bleach from a neighbor's laundry vent that sent him into a full panic attack in his own driveway. He stood there, hands shaking, unable to convince himself that he was not being gassed. That night, he told his wife he would make an appointment. He is afraid-afraid that the therapist will tell him he is overreacting, afraid that the fear will never stop, and, most quietly of all, afraid that something is still wrong with him that no one can find. But he is also tired. He hopes, somewhere beneath the vigilance, that he might one day sit still without wondering if the air is safe to breathe.
